segments.translit: paramakaruṇāsavapānataḥ(ṇata) pramudito hi kaṅkaṇasiddhācārya(ryo)s tam evārthaṃ śabdāntareṇa vyutpādayati |
segments.translation: Delighted by drinking the [liquor]{asava} of supreme [compassion]{karuna}, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Kaṅkaṇa]{p-kankana} sets out that same meaning in other words.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.44.m1) introduces the song: the [siddha]{siddha} master Kaṅkaṇa, delighted by drinking the [liquor]{asava} of supreme compassion, sets out the same meaning in other words. Where he has liquor (āsava), the Tibetan has nectar (bdud rtsi), and it calls the poet keng rus zhabs, 'skeleton', as if reading kaṅkāla.

flags.note: Where Munidatta (cp.44.m1) has āsava, 'liquor', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bdud rtsi, 'nectar', its usual word for amṛta: mchog gi snying rje'i bdud rtsi'i btung bas rab tu tshim pa, 'fully satisfied by drinking the nectar of supreme compassion', with tshim pa, 'satisfied', for pramudita, 'delighted'. The intoxication of the Sanskrit becomes nectar; I translate the Sanskrit. The Tibetan also calls the poet keng rus zhabs, 'skeleton', as if reading kaṅkāla for kaṅkaṇa, though its heading has kaM ka Na and its comment on 5a kaM ka na (cp.44.m6).

For tam evārthaṃ, 'that same meaning' (cp.44.m1), the Tibetan has de kho na nyid kyi don, which would normally mean 'the meaning of reality' (tattva) but may be an over-literal rendering of tam eva, 'just that'; it does the same in cp.44.m3. I follow the Sanskrit. It has gsungs, 'spoke', for vyutpādayati, 'sets out, explains'.
Shastri's parentheses in cp.44.m1, pānataḥ(ṇata) and -ācārya(ryo)s, record a variant or a correction; neither changes the sense ('from drinking'; 'the siddha master', nominative).

segments.translit: sune ityādi | tṛtīyasvādhiṣṭhānaśūnye vajraguroś cādhiṣṭhānāc caturtha[ṃ] pada[ṃ] śūnyaṃ [ya]dā mīlati svayaṃ tadā tasmin samaye | sarvadharmam iti yuganaddhaphalodayo bhavatīti |
segments.translation: 'With [emptiness]{sunyata}…' and so on: when the fourth state, [emptiness]{sunyata}, meets of itself with the third emptiness, that of [self-blessing]{svadhisthana}, and through the [blessing]{adhisthana} of the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}; then, at that moment. 'All [dharmas]{dharma}' means that the arising of the [fruit]{phala}, [coupled union]{yuganaddha}, comes about.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.44.m2) reads the two emptinesses of 1a as the third and the fourth: through the vajra guru's blessing, the fourth state, emptiness, meets of itself with the third, [self-blessing]{svadhisthana} (the Tibetan has only 'blessing'). He takes 1b's dhāma as 'all dharmas', as the Tibetan does, and their rising as the arising of the fruit, [coupled union]{yuganaddha}.

equations.en: with the third emptiness, that of self-blessing (tṛtīyasvādhiṣṭhānaśūnya)
the fourth state, emptiness (caturthaṃ padaṃ śūnyam), meeting it through the vajra guru's blessing
all dharmas (sarvadharma); their rising is the arising of the fruit, coupled union (yuganaddhaphalodaya)

flags.note: In cp.44.m2 the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has byin gyis brlabs pa stong pa, 'the emptiness of blessing', without rang, so it does not mark the third emptiness as self-blessing (svādhiṣṭhāna, regularly rang byin gyis brlabs pa); its manuscript may have read adhiṣṭhāna. It also has no word for 'third', unless gsungs pas, 'since it is said', after the lemma is a slip for gsum pa, 'third'. For mīlati, 'meets', it has mthun par byed pa, 'accords', as its line 1a has mthun gyur pa, and it seems to make rang nyid, 'oneself', the one who accords with the fourth state, where Munidatta's svayaṃ is 'of itself'. It agrees on chos thams cad, 'all dharmas'.

Munidatta's ca (cp.44.m2) joins a locative ('the third, self-blessing emptiness') and an ablative ('through the vajra guru's blessing'). I take the locative as what the fourth state meets, since mīl- takes the locative; it could instead give the place of the meeting: 'when, in the third emptiness …, the fourth state meets'.
Shastri's restorations in cp.44.m2, caturtha[ṃ] pada[ṃ] and [ya]dā, are secure in sense: the Tibetan has bzhi pa'i go 'phang, 'the fourth state', and gang gi tshe, 'when'.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena tam evārthaṃ kathayati—
caukhaṇam iti | tasmād vicitrādikṣaṇena caturthānandaṃ saṃbodhayitvā tiṣṭhāmi; tenāhaṃ madhyamānirodheti | saptaprakṛtidoṣāsamādhimalanidhānād anuttarabodhiṃ labhyate |
tathā ca dvikalpe—
ānandās tatra jāyanta ityādi [62ka]
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he tells the same meaning. 'The [four moments]{catuhksana}': so, having fully awakened the fourth [joy]{ananda} through the moments beginning with [vicitra]{vicitra}, I remain; by that I have '[cessation]{nirodha} in the [central channel]{madhyama}'. Through setting aside the faults of the seven [natures]{prakrti}, the [stains]{mala} of [samādhi]{samadhi}, [unsurpassed]{anuttara} [awakening]{bodhi} is gained. And so in the [Dvikalpa]{tx-hevajra}: 'There the [joys]{ananda} arise…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.44.m3) paraphrases the refrain: through the moments beginning with vicitra the speaker has fully awakened the fourth [joy]{ananda} and remains, and so has 'cessation in the madhyamā', the [central channel]{madhyama}, where the song says only mājha, 'middle'. Setting aside the faults of the seven natures, the stains of samādhi, gains unsurpassed awakening.

equations.en: the moments beginning with vicitra (vicitrādikṣaṇa), through which the fourth joy is fully awakened
the madhyamā, the central channel ('cessation in the madhyamā', madhyamānirodha, for mājha niroha)

citations.quoted: ānandās tatra jāyanta ityādi: 'There the joys arise…' and so on

flags.note: In cp.44.m3 the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) cites the lemma as skad cig bzhi pa, 'the fourth moment', though its line 2a has skad cig bzhi, 'four moments'. Where Shastri prints tiṣṭhāmi; tenāhaṃ, 'I remain; by that I', it has rang byin gyis brlabs pas, 'by self-blessing', and no first person: its manuscript may have read something like svādhiṣṭhānena. It agrees on dbu mar 'gog pa, 'cessation in the central channel'. It renders saptaprakṛtidoṣa- as an instrumental, rang bzhin bdun gyi nyes pas, 'by the faults of the seven natures', and nidhāna as gzhi, 'ground, basis'.

nidhāna in cp.44.m3: I take it as 'setting aside' (ni-dhā, 'lay down, put away'), so that unsurpassed awakening is gained by putting the faults away. It can also mean 'store, receptacle', which the Tibetan gzhi, 'ground', follows ('from the ground of the stains of samādhi unsurpassed awakening is obtained'); a reading nidhana, 'destruction', would give much my sense. I divide doṣāsamādhimala as doṣāḥ samādhimalāḥ, 'the faults, stains of samādhi', with the Tibetan and with Munidatta's 'seven faults, stains of samādhi' in cp.12.m2; doṣa-asamādhi-, 'faults, non-absorption', is also possible.

tenāhaṃ madhyamānirodheti (cp.44.m3) has no verb: 'by that I [have] cessation in the madhyamā', or 'I [am] cessation…'. anuttarabodhiṃ labhyate puts an accusative with a passive verb; I render 'is gained'.

For the draft's 2a: Munidatta (cp.44.m3) makes the moments the means (vicitrādikṣaṇena, 'through the moments beginning with vicitra') and the fourth joy what is fully awakened (caturthānandaṃ saṃbodhayitvā). The draft's 'having fully realized the four moments' makes the moments the object. The Tibetan line, skad cig bzhi la yang dag rtogs, 'fully realized in (or at) the four moments', is closer to him.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena abhyāsam āha—
nādam ityādi dīrghahūṃkāro nāpāyagrāhakajñānavikalpaṃ bindur iti | prajñāgrāhyajñānavikalpaḥ nādaḥ | etad ubhayaṃ vikalpena tasmin samaye parityakto(ktā)'smi | ataḥ sarvadharmānupalambhaṃ paśyan cittabodhanañ ca praṇaṣṭaṃ mama (ne) |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he states [practice]{abhyasa}. '[Nāda]{nada}…' and so on: the long [hūṃ]{hum}, the [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of cognition as [means]{upaya}, the grasper, is the '[drop]{bindu}'. [Nāda]{nada} is the conceptual thought of cognition as [wisdom]{prajna}, the grasped. At that moment I have given up both of these, as conceptual thought. So, seeing the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all [dharmas]{dharma}, my awakening of [mind]{citta} too has vanished.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.44.m4) calls this couplet practice. The drop is the long [hūṃ]{hum}, the conceptual thought of cognition as means, the grasper; nāda is that of cognition as wisdom, the grasped. At that moment the speaker has given up both as conceptual thought; seeing that no dharma is apprehended, the speaker's awakening of mind has vanished too.

equations.en: the long hūṃ, the conceptual thought of cognition as means, the grasper
the conceptual thought of cognition as wisdom, the grasped

flags.note: In cp.44.m4 Shastri prints nāpāyagrāhaka-. I read upāya-, 'means', with the Tibetan thabs 'dzin pa'i and the parallel prajñā-, 'wisdom', in the next sentence. The na- is perhaps a misreading or a stray syllable; dīrghahūṃkāra upāya- would be the regular sandhi.

Two parses of Munidatta's first gloss (cp.44.m4): (a) the long hūṃ and the conceptual thought of means are together said to be the bindu, as I translate, following the nominative dīrghahūṃkāraḥ and the Tibetan (hUM yig ring po thabs 'dzin pa'i … la thig le zhes so), which runs on without a break; (b) 'nāda and so on' concerns the long hūṃ, whose bindu (the dot) and nāda (the stroke above it) are then explained. Either way he makes bindu and nāda kinds of conceptual thought. I take upāyagrāhaka- and prajñāgrāhya- in parallel, 'means, the grasper' and 'wisdom, the grasped'; 'cognition that grasps means' and 'cognition grasped by wisdom' are also possible.

parityakto(ktā)'smi (cp.44.m4) is literally 'I am abandoned'. I take it actively, 'I have given up', as the Tibetan spong ba does (without a first person); it could also mean 'I have been left by both of these'. The parenthetical ktā gives a feminine form; nothing else in the comment marks the speaker as a woman.

mama (ne) in cp.44.m4: Shastri prints mama, 'my', with (ne) beside it. If the original was manye, 'I consider', the participle paśyan would have its verb: 'seeing the non-apprehension of all dharmas, I consider the awakening of mind too vanished'. The Tibetan ends mos pa'o, 'regards, is convinced', which supports something like manye, and it renders praṇaṣṭa as so sor mi dmigs pa, 'not apprehended individually'. I translate the printed mama.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) introduces the couplet as goms pa'i 'bras bu, 'the fruit of practice', where Munidatta's Sanskrit (cp.44.m4) has abhyāsam, 'practice'; compare abhyāsaphala in cp.20.m5.

For the draft's 3a ('here', Shastri's ṇahim̐ e; the Tibetan line has snying la, 'in the heart', as if dividing ṇa hie[m̐]): Munidatta's wording (cp.44.m4) does not decide it, but leans toward Shastri's text. He has no word for 'heart', though he renders hiem̐ as hṛdaya in cp.28.m6, and his 'at that moment' (tasmin samaye) could answer to e, 'this'; it may also simply repeat his phrase from cp.44.m2. 'Have not entered' becomes 'I have given up', which fits either reading.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena saṃvṛtibodhicittasya phāratām āha—
yathetyādi | ādau yasmād bodhicittād utpanno 'si tasmin nijabodhicitte induviṣayavikalpavirahite yac ca[tu]rtha sukhasaṃvedanarūpa[ṃ] jānīhi |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ—
jaṃ diṭa cia viloa ṭāu pavane samarasa hohī |
indi ṣaa auā sandhia anne kisame saṃbohi ||
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he states the spreading forth of [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}. 'Where…' and so on: in the bodhicitta from which you were born in the beginning, your own bodhicitta, free of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} about the [senses]{indriya} and [sense objects]{visaya}, know what has the form of the experience of the fourth [bliss]{sukha}. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha}: 'Where the [mind]{citta}, made firm, is turned back and becomes of the [same taste]{samarasa} with the [wind]{vayu}, where senses and objects come together and are joined: by what else is there [awakening]{bodhi}?'
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.44.m5) says this couplet shows the spreading forth of conventional [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, and comments only on 4a: where you came from is the bodhicitta from which you were first born; there, in your own bodhicitta, free of conceptual thought about senses and objects, you are to know the experience of the fourth bliss. He adds a verse of Saraha.

equations.en: the bodhicitta from which you were first born … in that, your own bodhicitta

citations.quoted: jaṃ diṭa cia viloa ṭāu pavane samarasa hohī | indi ṣaa auā sandhia anne kisame saṃbohi: 'Where the mind, made firm, is turned back and becomes of the same taste with the wind, where senses and objects come together and are joined: by what else is there awakening?'
citations.work: a verse of Saraha (work not named; perhaps one of his dohā collections)

flags.note: phāratā in cp.44.m5 is unclear. I take it as sphāratā, 'spreading, expanse' (compare Old Bengali phar-, 'radiate', in song 42). The Tibetan has byed pa nyid, 'agency, activity', as if reading something like kāritā; that would suit his point that one was born from bodhicitta.

induviṣayavikalpa in cp.44.m5: indu, 'moon', makes little sense here. I read indriya, 'senses', with the Tibetan dbang po dang yul gyi rnam par rtog pa, 'conceptual thought of senses and objects', and with indi in the Saraha verse that follows. In ca[tu]rtha the [tu] is Shastri's restoration, supported by the Tibetan bzhi pa'i, 'of the fourth'.

For sukhasaṃvedanarūpa, 'having the form of the experience of bliss' (cp.44.m5), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bde ba rang rig pa'i ngo bo, 'the nature of self-awareness of bliss', as if reading svasaṃvedana; for jānīhi, 'know!', it has shes pa'i phyir ro, 'because one knows'. Otherwise its comment agrees, including dang po gang las … de la, 'from which at first … in that'.

The Saraha verse in cp.44.m5 is Apabhraṃśa and partly corrupt; my rendering leans on the Tibetan. diṭa as diḍha, 'firm' (Tibetan brtan); viloa as viloma, 'turned back' (rnam bzlog); ṭāu perhaps ṭhāu, 'place'; indi as indriya (dbang po); ṣaa uncertain (visaa, 'objects'? the Tibetan has yul, 'objects', and mtshungs nyid, 'sameness'); auā sandhia perhaps 'come and joined'; anne kisame saṃbohi as 'by what else is there awakening?', where the Tibetan has gzhan du gang gis mtshungs pa nyid du 'gyur, 'by what else would it become sameness?'.

For the draft's couplet 4: Munidatta's yasmāt … tasmin (cp.44.m5) supports reading jathām̐ … tathā as source and place, 'where you came from … there', against the Tibetan line's manner and result (ji ltar 'ongs pa de ltar shes par gyur, 'as one came, so one came to know'); his utpanno 'si supports the second person and jānīhi the imperative 'know'. He names what is to be known, the experience of the fourth bliss, where the draft has 'it'. He does not cite or gloss 4b: nothing in his comment answers to মাসং ('middle' in the draft) or থাকী, and বিহাণ is echoed at most by his virahita, 'free of' (compare vihīna, 'devoid of'). The draft's 'middle' and 'left behind' rest on the Tibetan line alone (dbu ma ru … rnam par spong).

segments.translit:
caturthapadena svakīyaprabhā[vaṃ] pratipādayati—
bhaṇai ityādi | kaṅkaṇapādasiddhācāryo hi vadati | sākāranirākārādi bālayogināṃ kalakalaḥ samatathatānādena bhagnaḥ |
tathā cāgamaḥ |—
śūnyatāsiṃhanādena trāsitāḥ sarvaśatruvaḥ || 44 ||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he sets out his own [power]{prabhava}. 'Kaṅkaṇa says…' and so on: the [siddha]{siddha} master [Kaṅkaṇapāda]{p-kankana} says: the [clamour]{kalakala} of [novice yogins]{balayogin} over '[with form and formless]{sakara-nirakara}' and the like is shattered by the sound of sameness and [suchness]{tathata}. And so the [scripture]{agama}: 'By the [lion's roar]{simhanada} of [emptiness]{sunyata} all enemies are terrified.'
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.44.m6) says the last couplet sets out Kaṅkaṇa's own power. His paraphrase makes the [clamour]{kalakala} the thing shattered: the clamour of novice yogins over 'with form', 'formless' and the like is broken by the sound of sameness and suchness (Tibetan: 'the unstruck sound of sameness'), as a scripture says the lion's roar of emptiness terrifies all enemies.

equations.en: the sound of sameness and suchness (samatathatānāda), which shatters the clamour of novice yogins

citations.quoted: śūnyatāsiṃhanādena trāsitāḥ sarvaśatruvaḥ: 'By the lion's roar of emptiness all enemies are terrified'

flags.note: In cp.44.m6 the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mnyam pa nyid gzhom du med pa'i sgra yis bcom pa, 'destroyed by the sound of sameness, the unstruck', where Munidatta has samatathatānāda, 'the sound of sameness and suchness': it has the unstruck (anāhata) and no word for suchness, though its line 5b has both (de nyid gzhom med dbyangs). Its ca co, 'noise, chatter', agrees with kalakala. Its line 5a reads ka la ya as a name and sādem̐ as drin, 'grace', as if prasāda: 'Kaṅkaṇa says: by the grace of Kalaya'. Munidatta's paraphrase gives no support to a name.
svakīyaprabhā[vaṃ] in cp.44.m6 is Shastri's restoration. The Tibetan rang nyid kyi mthu, 'his own power' (mthu regularly renders prabhāva), supports it over prabhā, 'radiance'.

In the verse Munidatta quotes (cp.44.m6) the Tibetan has sgra rnams thams cad, 'all sounds', for sarvaśatravaḥ, 'all enemies', probably a slip of sgra for dgra, 'enemy', under the preceding sgra; read as it stands, the roar would silence all other sounds. The printed śatruvaḥ is an irregular plural for śatravaḥ.

For the draft's 5a: Munidatta's paraphrase (cp.44.m6) makes the clamour (kalakala, the song's kalaela) the subject of 'shattered' (bhagna, for biccharila in 5b), so that the clamorous sound is what is destroyed, not the manner of Kaṅkaṇa's speech. The draft's 'with a clamour of sound' leaves this open. The instrumental -em̐ of sādem̐ fits the draft's 'with'; Munidatta restructures the couplet, so this is his reading, not proof of the syntax.

questions: 3a, 'here' or 'in the heart' (cp.44.m4): Munidatta's comment has no word for either. Since he renders hiem̐ as hṛdaya in cp.28.m6, his silence leans toward Shastri's ṇahim̐ e, but does not settle it. Keep the draft's 'here', with a witness flag for the Tibetan snying la (as if ṇa hie[m̐])?

Couplet 4 (cp.44.m5): his yasmāt … tasmin and jānīhi support 'Where you came from, know it there' (source and place; imperative), and he names what is to be known. He does not comment on 4b, so 'middle' (মাসং) and 'left behind' (বিহাণ) rest on the Tibetan line alone (dbu ma ru … rnam par spong); his virahita, 'free of', may echo বিহাণ. Should the draft's 4b carry a flag saying so?

5a (cp.44.m6): his paraphrase makes the clamour the thing shattered in 5b. Should 5a–5b be punctuated to allow 'Kaṅkaṇa says: the clamour of sound, all of it, has been shattered…', or keep the draft's open 'with a clamour of sound' and leave his reading to the note?
2a (cp.44.m3): he makes the four moments the means and the fourth joy the object; the draft makes the moments the object. Worth a note on the line?

cp.44.m2: the third emptiness (self-blessing) meeting the fourth state and yielding coupled union matches the order of the Pañcakrama's stages three, four and five (self-blessing, clear light, coupled union). Munidatta does not name clear light here, so I kept it out of the note. Should a note mention the scheme, attributed to the system and not to him?

cp.44.m4: translate the printed mama ('my'), as I did, or adopt manye ('I consider'), which the grammar and the Tibetan mos pa'o favour? And do you prefer my parse of the long hūṃ (it is the bindu) or the alternative (the long hūṃ is the topic, bindu and nāda its parts)?

cp.44.m5: the Saraha verse is rendered tentatively from a corrupt Apabhraṃśa text with the Tibetan's help, and phāratā ('spreading forth') is a guess. Would you rather mark the obscure words as untranslated?

cp.44.m3: the quotation is from the Hevajra, which Munidatta cites as the Dvikalpa. From memory the half-verse goes on kṣaṇabhedena lakṣitāḥ, on the moments, but I have not checked it. I used the surface 'Dvikalpa' with the id tx-hevajra, whose approved English is 'Hevajra'; change it if titles must use the approved form.

Equations (cp.44.m2–m6): besides the iti-glosses (caukhaṇa, bindu, nāda, dhāma as sarvadharma), I listed word-for-word paraphrase glosses (sune, suna, jathām̐ … tathā, tadhatānādem̐) and mājha as madhyamā, which the majha entry now calls 'no explicit gloss'. I left kalaela out for the same reason. Prune any you do not count as explicit.
